chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Qasim ibn Yahya, from his grandfather al-Hasan ibn Rashid, from Ya'qub ibn Ja'far ibn Ibrahim al-Ja'fari, who said:
The beauty of peacocks was mentioned in the presence of Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), and he said: 'It would not surpass for you the beauty of the white rooster in anything.'

He said: And I heard him saying: 'The rooster has a better voice than the peacock, and it is greater in blessing; it alerts you at the times of the salat, whereas the peacock cries out in lamentation because of the sin with which it has been afflicted.'

key_terms.الدِّيكُ الْأَبْيَضُ: The white rooster, praised for alerting worshippers to prayer times
key_terms.الْخَطِيئَةُ: The sin/error, the primordial mistake the peacock committed
key_terms.الْوَيْلُ: Woe/lamentation, here the peacock's cry interpreted as a mournful lament
key_terms.حُسْنُ الطَّاوُسِ: The beauty of the peacock, used as a symbol of outward appearances
key_terms.مَوَاقِيتُ الصَّلَاةِ: The times of the salat (prayer), the prescribed prayer intervals

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Kazim say about the rooster and the peacock?
ai.summary: Imam Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) — most likely Imam al-Kazim — was asked about the beauty of peacocks and redirected attention to the white rooster, which he praised as superior in voice and greater in blessing. The Imam explained that the rooster's practical utility — waking believers for prayer — made it spiritually superior to the merely beautiful peacock. According to this tradition, the peacock's cry is interpreted as a lament for a primordial sin it committed, a cosmological detail that explains its plaintive call and reinforces the teaching that spiritual usefulness outweighs superficial beauty.
